quote: I haven't done it because I figured it'd be expensive to do.
stewart_read: This is a textbook trigger for the bill-swap flip — 'what's expensive is your current bill, not solar' — but the rep answers with a generic incentives pitch instead of anchoring to Robert's own soon-to-be-known PSO bill.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep may have deliberately deferred the deep cost conversation to avoid setter scope creep, planning to let the closer handle it with real numbers.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to hold the cost fear in mind and circle back to it once the bill number is captured, using the customer's own figure as the flip.

quote: the requirements to qualify are to have a form of taxable income and a credit score of six fifty or higher.
stewart_read: Schema states the credit threshold is 670; this rep states 650, matching the same drift already logged in SESSION18_fcbf33c1. This is a second data point suggesting either the active policy has genuinely moved to 650 or reps are inconsistently trained on the number.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep could be intentionally using a lower buffer number to avoid DQ'ing borderline customers, but there's no evidence of deliberate strategy here — it reads as the number he was trained on.
coaching_implication: Flag for reconciliation with Kenny: two independent reps now stating 650 instead of the schema's 670 — worth confirming whether the schema is stale or the reps need correction.

quote: I think I have, like, a six zero four. My wife has a higher one. She's close to 700, and she's on she's on the mortgage too.
stewart_read: Customer discloses his own credit score is below even the stated 650 threshold, but the rep immediately pivots to the wife's higher score and title status to keep qualification alive rather than probing or flagging this clearly for the closer.
alternative_hypothesis: This could be correct triage — using the co-owner's stronger credit to qualify the household is a legitimate move, not a miss, since Ion's requirement is about the household qualifying, not each individual.
coaching_implication: Reasonable in the moment, but the handoff brief must flag Robert's stated 604 explicitly so the closer isn't surprised at credit-pull time.

quote: Well, so it's been winter. We just bought the house, two months ago, and, everything in it is primarily gas.
stewart_read: Customer gives context that undercuts the bill number just captured (new home, gas-heavy, winter) — a rich moment to note but the rep doesn't press for a summer estimate or explicitly capture the usage trajectory, just acknowledges and moves on.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep may be trusting the design team to project usage from the utility bill data directly rather than needing a verbal summer estimate on the call.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to ask one more question here — 'do you have a sense of what the previous owners paid in summer?' — since seasonal variance materially affects the pitch.

quote: But with summertime, I don't know how high it'll be because they see and all that.
stewart_read: Customer flags that summer AC load will likely push the bill well above the current $100-200 winter range — this is a forward-looking usage increase signal the rep could anchor on ('so this could be a good amount higher come summer, which is exactly when solar helps most').
coaching_implication: Point out to the rep that customer-volunteered future-usage-increase signals are gold for the pitch — reflect them back rather than letting them pass as small talk.

quote: the thing about it is me and my wife both work night shift.
stewart_read: Customer discloses a genuinely constrained schedule (night shift, kids, narrow afternoon window); rep handles this well by working within the stated window rather than pushing a standard slot.
coaching_implication: This is a positive handling — no coaching correction needed, but the handoff brief should carry the night-shift constraint forward so the closer doesn't default to an evening call attempt.

quote: Well, that's been my biggest concern is I always heard how expensive it was... for the panels and the batteries and all the things.
stewart_read: The customer restates his opening cost fear almost verbatim at the very end of the call, right before hangup, and the rep again responds with a vague 'cool to see the programs' line rather than directly flipping it with the bill number already on record.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep may be intentionally leaving the substantive cost conversation for the closer's appointment rather than re-litigating it on the setter call — consistent with setter_scope_discipline.
coaching_implication: Even holding scope discipline, a 10-second flip ('that's exactly why we look at your PSO bill — most people find the swap is less than what they're already paying') would have closed the loop before handoff instead of leaving the fear open.
